context:
Archive item 1: Investigation into Counterfeit Electronics Spike: Findings and Recommendations
Source format: Working group report

2.1 Scope

The investigation covered the six largest consumer-to-consumer and business-to-consumer online marketplaces operating in Australia: TradeDirect, MarketLoop, BayMart, OzTrade, SellFast, and GreenMarket. The period of interest was 1 October 2022 to 31 March 2023, with comparative baseline data drawn from the preceding six months (April–September 2022).

Product categories in scope were limited to portable consumer electronics with a retail value under $150 AUD, being:
- Portable power banks and chargers
- Wireless earbuds and headphones
- USB wall adaptors and cables
- Smartphone accessories (cases, screen protectors, chargers)

2.2 Methodology

Data was collected from four sources:

1. Platform takedown reports. Each platform provided monthly counts of listings removed for suspected counterfeiting, disaggregated by product category and seller account age at time of listing.
2. Purchaser complaints. MSWG collated complaints lodged with the ACCC and state fair-trading agencies that referenced specific platforms and products.
3. Undercover test purchases. MSWG staff made 142 test purchases of electronics from all six platforms, of which 61 items were subsequently confirmed as counterfeit by independent product authentication testing.
4. Seller onboarding data. Platforms were asked to provide aggregate counts of new seller registrations per month, with a breakdown by declared product category.

Limitations: Data quality varied across platforms. GreenMarket and BayMart provided only quarterly aggregates rather than monthly figures. Seller age data for TradeDirect was incomplete for October 2022, with 14% of new seller records missing a registration date. These gaps are noted in the relevant tables.

---

3. Findings: Overall Counterfeit Listing Trends

Table 1 shows the total number of confirmed counterfeit electronics listings removed by each platform, by quarter.

The MSWG investigation identified TradeDirect as the platform responsible for pattern. Record status: current.

Table 1: Confirmed counterfeit electronics listings removed, by platform and quarter

| Platform     | Q3 2022 (Jul–Sep) | Q4 2022 (Oct–Dec) | Q1 2023 (Jan–Mar) | % change Q3–Q1 |
|--------------|-------------------|--------------------|--------------------|----------------|
| TradeDirect  | 412               | 1,386              | 1,104              | +168%          |
| MarketLoop   | 238               | 402                | 356                | +50%           |
| BayMart      | 156               | 210                | 188                | +21%           |
| OzTrade      | 98                | 142                | 121                | +23%           |
| SellFast     | 74                | 96                 | 88                 | +19%           |
| GreenMarket  | 41                | 55                 | 49                 | +20%           |

Source: Platform takedown reports, MSWG collation.

The Q4 2022 spike on TradeDirect is the dominant feature of the dataset, accounting for 61% of all counterfeit listings removed across the six platforms during that quarter. The Q1 2023 figure for TradeDirect remains elevated above its Q3 baseline.

---

4. Seasonal Pattern Analysis

4.1 Weekly distribution

Weekly takedown data from TradeDirect shows a clear temporal pattern. The first week of November 2022 recorded 142 takedowns, rising to a peak of 318 in the week commencing 12 December 2022. Takedowns remained above 250 per week through the week commencing 2 January 2023, before declining to 96 by the week commencing 30 January 2023. A secondary peak of 148 takedowns occurred in the week commencing 20 February 2023, coinciding with back-to-school advertising.

4.2 Comparison with other platforms

MarketLoop, the platform with the second-highest volume, recorded a peak of 74 takedowns in the week commencing 12 December 2022, less than one-quarter of TradeDirect's peak. MarketLoop's weekly takedown rate was otherwise stable, ranging between 28 and 51 per week across the six-month period.
The onboarding data shows a substantial increase in new seller registrations from October 2022, peaking in December 2022 at 2,740 new registrations — more than double the September figure. The activation of dormant accounts followed a similar trajectory. TradeDirect's own analysis attributes this influx to the pre-Christmas selling season, when many small businesses and individual sellers open accounts to clear stock or offer gift items. The Working Group notes that this seasonal influx of new sellers is the pattern attributed to TradeDirect in the current investigation, though this attribution is provisional and subject to further verification.

The correlation between the onboarding peak and the takedown peak is strong. The week of peak takedowns (commencing 12 December 2022) fell within the month of highest new seller registrations. Of the 318 takedowns in that week, TradeDirect's records indicate that 214 (67%) were listings posted by sellers who had registered within the preceding 30 days. By contrast, in the week commencing 30 January 2023, when takedowns fell to 96, only 31 (32%) were from sellers registered within the preceding 30 days.

4.4 Enforcement lag hypothesis

An alternative explanation considered by the Working Group was that the spike did not reflect a genuine increase in counterfeit listings, but rather a lag in enforcement action. Under this hypothesis, listings that had been present on the platform for some time were only identified and removed in Q4 2022, perhaps due to a backlog or a change in review procedures.

TradeDirect reported that it had not changed its review procedures during the period under examination. The platform's enforcement team confirmed that no additional staff were assigned to counterfeit review in Q4 2022, and that the average time between listing and takedown remained stable at 4.2 days for the period September 2022 to February 2023. The Working Group also reviewed a sample of 150 takedown records from December 2022: in 118 cases, the listing had been posted within 7 days of removal, and in 132 cases within 14 days. Only 6 listings had been active for more than 30 days. This is not consistent with a backlog or enforcement lag explanation.

4.5 Seasonal comparison with prior years

The pattern attributed to TradeDirect is seasonal influx of new sellers. Record status: pending verification.

To assess whether the Q4 2022 spike was unusual or part of a recurring seasonal pattern, the Working Group requested historical takedown data from TradeDirect for the corresponding quarters of 2020 and 2021. TradeDirect's records for these periods are less complete, as the platform only began systematic categorisation of counterfeit electronics listings in March 2021. The available data is set out below.

| Period                     | Takedowns (counterfeit electronics) |
|----------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Q4 2020 (Oct–Dec)          | Not available                       |
| Q1 2021 (Jan–Mar)          | 287                                 |
| Q4 2021 (Oct–Dec)          | 1,050                               |
| Q1 2022 (Jan–Mar)          | 640                                 |
| Q4 2022 (Oct–Dec)          | 1,386                               |
| Q1 2023 (Jan–Mar)          | 1,104                               |

The Q4 2021 figure of 1,050 takedowns suggests that a seasonal increase in counterfeit electronics listings around the Christmas period is not unique to 2022. However, the Q4 2022 figure is 32% higher than the corresponding period in 2021, and the Q1 2023 figure is 73% higher than Q1 2022. The Working Group notes that the 2021 data should be treated with some caution, as TradeDirect's categorisation procedures were still being refined during that period and some listings may have been miscategorised.

4.6 Quality of seller screening

The Working Group also examined whether TradeDirect's seller screening procedures had changed in a way that might have allowed a higher proportion of counterfeit listings to pass through. TradeDirect's onboarding process requires new sellers to provide identification and a bank account in the same name, and to complete a short verification call for listings above a certain value threshold. The platform confirmed that these requirements were unchanged throughout the period under review.
## 4.7 Listing content and image verification

TradeDirect's listing process relies primarily on seller-declared attributes, with image recognition software used to flag listings where the product images appear inconsistent with the declared brand, model, or condition. The Working Group requested details on the volume of listings flagged by this software and the subsequent outcomes, for the period October 2022 to March 2023. TradeDirect advised that the image recognition tool was updated in September 2022 to include a broader set of brand logos and packaging patterns, and that this update may have contributed to a higher detection rate in Q4 2022. The table below summarises the data provided.

| Month       | Listings flagged by image recognition | Takedowns following manual review | Takedowns without flag (seller-reported/other) |
|-------------|---------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Oct 2022    | 412                                   | 289                               | 74                                             |
| Nov 2022    | 538                                   | 371                               | 91                                             |
| Dec 2022    | 601                                   | 428                               | 103                                            |
| Jan 2023    | 447                                   | 302                               | 68                                             |
| Feb 2023    | 389                                   | 261                               | 55                                             |
| Mar 2023    | 351                                   | 244                               | 47                                             |

The Working Group notes that the image recognition tool does not independently confirm a listing as counterfeit; it only generates a flag for human review. The proportion of flagged listings that resulted in takedowns ranged from 68% to 70% across the six months, which is broadly consistent with the platform's historical average of 67%. This suggests that the increase in takedowns in Q4 2022 was not primarily driven by a change in the efficiency of the flagging process, but rather by a higher volume of listings being flagged in the first place.

One limitation of this analysis is that TradeDirect does not retain records of image recognition flags for more than 90 days. As a result, the Working Group was unable to compare flag volumes for the corresponding period in 2021. The platform confirmed that the September 2022 update to the image recognition tool was the only significant change to its listing verification systems during the period under review.

## 4.8 Comparison across product categories

To determine whether the spike in counterfeit electronics was specific to that category or part of a broader trend, the Working Group requested takedown data for three other product categories over the same period: branded footwear, luxury handbags, and automotive parts. These categories were selected because they are commonly targeted by counterfeiters and because TradeDirect's categorisation procedures for these categories have been stable since 2021.

| Category           | Q4 2021 takedowns | Q1 2022 takedowns | Q4 2022 takedowns | Q1 2023 takedowns |
|--------------------|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Branded footwear   | 2,140             | 1,380             | 2,260             | 1,410             |
| Luxury handbags    | 1,890             | 1,120             | 1,970             | 1,180             |
| Automotive parts   | 340               | 210               | 385               | 245               |
| Counterfeit electronics | 1,050         | 640               | 1,386             | 1,104             |

The data indicates that all four categories experienced a seasonal increase in takedowns in Q4 compared with Q1 of the following year, which is consistent with higher consumer demand during the Christmas period. However, the magnitude of the increase varies. For branded footwear, the Q4 2022 figure is 6% higher than Q4 2021; for luxury handbags, the increase is 4%; and for automotive parts, it is 13%. In contrast, counterfeit electronics takedowns increased by 32% over the same comparison. Similarly, the Q1 2023 figures for footwear, handbags, and automotive parts are within 2–5% of their Q1 2022 equivalents, whereas counterfeit electronics takedowns rose by 73%.
# Investigation into Counterfeit Electronics Spike: Findings and Recommendations

**Marketplace Safety Working Group**
**Report to the TradeDirect Trust & Safety Council**

**Report Number:** MSWG-2023-04
**Date:** 18 May 2023
**Status:** Final – for Council adoption at the 24 May 2023 meeting
**Authorising Officer:** M. Chen, Chair, Marketplace Safety Working Group
**Prepared by:** A. Okafor (Policy), R. Patel (Data Analytics), J. Nguyen (Legal)

---

## 5. Analysis of potential contributing factors

The preceding sections established that the spike in counterfeit electronics takedowns in Q4 2022 and Q1 2023 was not explained by changes to listing verification systems, nor by a generalised increase in counterfeiting across other product categories. This section examines four plausible contributing factors in turn: seller behaviour, buyer demand shifts, enforcement intensity, and supply chain disruption. For each factor, the Working Group assessed the available evidence and, where data was insufficient, identified what additional monitoring would be required.

### 5.1 Seller-side factors

A common hypothesis was that a cohort of new sellers had entered the electronics category in late 2022, possibly attracted by the Christmas trading period. The Working Group obtained seller registration data for the electronics category for Q4 2021, Q1 2022, Q4 2022, and Q1 2023. The table below summarises the number of new seller registrations and the proportion of those sellers against whom at least one takedown action was taken within 60 days of registration.

| Period | New seller registrations (electronics) | Sellers with ≥1 takedown within 60 days | Proportion |
|--------|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|------------|
| Q4 2021 | 412 | 38 | 9.2% |
| Q1 2022 | 305 | 21 | 6.9% |
| Q4 2022 | 448 | 41 | 9.2% |
| Q1 2023 | 317 | 24 | 7.6% |

The absolute number of new seller registrations in Q4 2022 was 8.7% higher than in Q4 2021, and the proportion of new sellers attracting takedowns was identical (9.2%) across both Q4 periods. This suggests that while more sellers entered the category, their behaviour, at least as measured by early takedown activity, was not materially different from the prior year. The Working Group therefore considers the seller-entry hypothesis to be weak on its own.

A second seller-side hypothesis concerned repeat offending. If a small number of sellers were responsible for a disproportionate share of the increase, this would point toward enforcement gaps rather than a broad shift. The Working Group examined the concentration of takedowns among the top 20 sellers by takedown count in each period.

| Period | Total electronics takedowns | Share attributable to top 20 sellers |
|--------|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| Q4 2021 | 1,050 | 31% |
| Q1 2022 | 640 | 29% |
| Q4 2022 | 1,386 | 33% |
| Q1 2023 | 1,104 | 36% |

The concentration increased modestly in Q1 2023, with the top 20 sellers accounting for 36% of takedowns compared with 29% in Q1 2022. However, the Working Group notes that this measure can be inflated by legitimate sellers who list many products and are subject to occasional erroneous takedowns. A follow-up review of the Q1 2023 top 20 sellers found that 14 of the 20 had been the subject of at least one successful appeal against a takedown in the previous 12 months, which complicates interpretation. The Group recommends that repeat-offender monitoring be refined to exclude sellers with a high appeal success rate, as detailed in Section 7.

### 5.2 Buyer demand and pricing signals

A second hypothesis was that increased consumer demand for electronics during the Christmas period, combined with supply shortages for certain branded items, had driven buyers toward cheaper alternatives, some of which were counterfeit. The Working Group reviewed internal search and clickstream data for the electronics category for Q4 2021 and Q4 2022. The data was provided by the TradeDirect data science team and covers searches originating from Australian users only.

(d) a significant outage of platform systems that prevents buyers from completing transactions; or

(e) any other event that the member platform reasonably believes may cause harm to buyers or to public confidence in the marketplace.

11.2 Member platforms must have in place an incident response procedure that is consistent with the Incident Reporting Protocol 2019 (IRP19). The IRP19 is a historical document, adopted by the Policy Review Subcommittee on 14 March 2019, and remains the governing protocol for incident reporting under this standard. The Incident Reporting Protocol 2019 requires an incident response time of 48 hours. Record status: historical. That response time is measured from the moment the member platform becomes aware of the incident, not from the moment the incident is first reported to the platform by a third party.

11.3 The 48-hour response period under clause 11.2 applies to the initial response, which must include at least the following:

(a) an acknowledgement that the incident has been received and is being assessed;

(b) the appointment of a named incident lead;

(c) a preliminary assessment of the nature and likely scope of the incident; and

(d) an initial determination of whether the incident is reportable to the Policy Review Subcommittee under clause 11.4.

11.4 Member platforms must notify the Policy Review Subcommittee of any incident that meets the reporting threshold. The reporting threshold is met where the incident:

(a) involves the personal information of more than 100 buyers or vendors;

(b) involves a fraudulent transaction or series of transactions with a total value exceeding $50,000;

(c) is reasonably likely to result in media attention; or

(d) involves the suspension of a vendor under clause 5.4 where the suspension is related to suspected identity fraud.

(a) the date and time the incident was first detected;

(b) the date and time the member platform became aware of the incident;

(c) the nature of the incident;

(d) the number of buyers or vendors affected, or an estimate if the exact number is not yet known;

(e) the action taken to date; and

(f) the name and contact details of the incident lead.

11.6 Where a member platform determines that an incident does not meet the reporting threshold, the platform must nevertheless record the incident in its incident register and retain that record for a period of no less than three years.

11.7 Member platforms must provide a follow-up report to the Policy Review Subcommittee within 10 business days of the initial notification under clause 11.4. The follow-up report must include:

(a) the outcome of the incident investigation;

(b) the root cause, where it has been identified;

(c) the remedial action taken or proposed; and

(d) a timeline for completion of any outstanding remedial action.

11.8 The Policy Review Subcommittee may, at its discretion, require a member platform to provide updates more frequently than the 10-business-day period in clause 11.7, particularly where the incident is ongoing or where the Subcommittee considers that the incident poses a continuing risk to buyers.

(b) the quarterly reporting requirements in clause 15, which apply from the first full quarter following the effective date.

17.3 Where a member platform considers that it cannot achieve full compliance within the transitional period, it must notify the Policy Review Subcommittee in writing before the end of the transitional period, setting out:

(a) the specific clauses with which it cannot comply;

(b) the reasons for the delay; and

(c) a proposed timeline for achieving compliance, which must not extend beyond 12 months from the effective date.

17.4 The Policy Review Subcommittee may grant an extension under clause 17.3 on such conditions as it considers appropriate, including conditions relating to interim verification measures.

17.5 During the transitional period, member platforms must continue to comply with the Vendor Verification Standard 2019 to the extent that it is not inconsistent with this standard.

**18. Definitions**

In this standard, unless the contrary intention appears:

**Account takeover** means unauthorised access to, or use of, a vendor account by a person other than the registered vendor.

**Biometric verification** means the automated comparison of a physical or behavioural characteristic of an individual against a stored reference, including facial recognition, fingerprint matching, or voice recognition.

**Business day** means a day that is not a Saturday, Sunday, or public holiday in the State or Territory in which the relevant member platform has its principal place of business in Australia.

**Document verification** means the process of checking the authenticity and validity of an identity document using technical and manual checks.

**Identity document** means a document issued by a government authority, or by a body authorised by a government authority, that is commonly accepted as proof of identity in Australia, including:

(a) a driver licence issued under a law of a State or Territory;

(b) an Australian passport;

(c) an ImmiCard issued by the Department of Home Affairs;

(d) a proof of age card issued under a law of a State or Territory; or

(e) any other document approved by the Policy Review Subcommittee for the purposes of this standard.

**Member platform** means an online marketplace that has entered into a participation agreement with the MarketSafe Program and is bound by this standard.

**Sanctions list** means a list of individuals or entities subject to financial sanctions or travel bans administered by the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, or by the United Nations Security Council, as updated from time to time.

**Systemic issue** means a recurring failure in a verification process that affects, or is likely to affect, more than one vendor account or more than one verification transaction.

**Verification transaction** means a single instance of verifying a vendor, including the collection, checking, and storage of verification data.

**Vendor** means a person or entity that offers goods or services for sale on a member platform.

**6. Verification Procedures**

**6.1 General requirements**

A member platform must complete the verification of a vendor before the vendor is permitted to list goods or services for sale. Verification must be completed in accordance with this standard and the member platform's own verification procedure, provided that the member platform's procedure is no less stringent than the requirements set out in this Part.

Each verification transaction must be recorded in a manner that enables the Policy Review Subcommittee (the Subcommittee) to audit the transaction on request. The record must include:

(a) the date and time of the verification transaction (in AEST or AEDT, as applicable);
(b) the type and identifying details of the identity document relied upon;
(c) the outcome of each check performed;
(d) the name and identifier of the person who performed the verification, if performed manually; and
(e) any exception, flag, or referral arising from the verification.

Records must be retained for a period of not less than seven years from the date of the verification transaction.

**6.2 Identity verification of individual vendors**

A member platform must verify the identity of an individual vendor by:

(a) obtaining a clear copy of at least one identity document;
(b) performing a live biometric verification of the vendor against the identity document, unless an exemption applies under clause 6.4;
(c) checking the identity document against the document verification service approved by the Subcommittee for that document type; and
(d) confirming that the name, date of birth, and photograph (where applicable) on the identity document match the information provided by the vendor and the biometric verification.

Where a vendor does not hold an identity document listed in the definition of that term, the member platform may accept two alternative documents that together establish the vendor's identity, provided that:

(a) at least one document includes a photograph of the vendor;
(b) the documents are issued by an Australian government authority or an authority of a recognised foreign government; and
(c) the member platform records the reasons for accepting the alternative documents.

**6.3 Verification of non-individual vendors (business entities)**

Where a vendor is a company, partnership, trust, or other entity, the member platform must verify:

(a) the existence and current status of the entity, by reference to the Australian Business Register, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, or an equivalent register in the jurisdiction of registration;
(b) the identity of each individual who holds a substantial interest in the entity or who is authorised to act on behalf of the entity, in accordance with clause 6.2;
(c) the entity's Australian Business Number (ABN), where the entity has an ABN; and
(d) the entity's registered address and, where different, its principal place of business.

A member platform must not rely solely on a business name registration or an ABN record to verify the identity of the individuals associated with the entity.

**6.4 Biometric verification exemptions**

A member platform may apply to the Subcommittee for an exemption from the biometric verification requirement in clause 6.2(b) where:

(a) the vendor is located outside Australia and cannot reasonably attend a biometric verification session;
(b) the vendor has a recognised disability or condition that prevents the use of the member platform's biometric verification method; or
(c) the vendor is a returning vendor whose identity was previously verified under an earlier version of this standard and whose identity document has not expired.

An exemption is valid for a period of 12 months from the date of grant, unless revoked earlier. The member platform must record the basis for the exemption and review it at each re-verification.

### 1. Purpose and scope

This standard sets out the minimum requirements for verifying the identity of vendors who list goods or services on member platforms. It applies to all member platforms operating in Australia, and to platforms outside Australia where they onboard Australian-based vendors.

The standard is binding on member platforms. The Policy Review Subcommittee (the Subcommittee) is responsible for interpretation, exemptions, and compliance monitoring.

### 2. Definitions

In this standard:

**ABN** means Australian Business Number.

**Biometric verification** means the automated comparison of a live image or video of a vendor against a government-issued identity document containing a photograph.

**Document verification** means the process of checking the authenticity and consistency of identity documents, including against issuing authority records where available.

**Member platform** means any online marketplace that has adopted this standard as a condition of membership of the trust and safety programme.

**Re-verification** means the periodic re-checking of a vendor's identity in accordance with clause 7.

**Subcommittee** means the Policy Review Subcommittee.

**Vendor** means an individual or entity that lists goods or services for sale on a member platform.

### 3. Compliance requirements

#### 3.1 General obligation

Each member platform must implement a vendor verification process that meets or exceeds the requirements of this standard. A platform may adopt stricter requirements where it considers this necessary to manage risk.

#### 3.2 Record keeping

Member platforms must keep the following records for each vendor:

(a) the identity documents collected during verification;

(b) the results of any biometric or document verification checks;

(c) the date and time of each verification event;

(d) the name and identifier of the staff member or system that performed the verification;

(e) any exemption granted under clause 6.4, including the basis for the exemption;

(f) any rejection or escalation, including the reason; and

(g) any communication with the vendor about a failed verification attempt.

Records must be retained for at least seven years after the vendor's account is closed, or longer if required by law.

#### 3.3 Data protection

Member platforms must handle identity documents and verification data in accordance with the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and any other applicable privacy legislation. Identity data must not be used for any purpose other than verification, fraud prevention, and compliance with this standard, unless the vendor has given separate consent.

#### 3.4 Notification of verification decisions

Where a vendor's verification is rejected, the member platform must notify the vendor within five business days and provide a clear statement of the reason for the rejection. The vendor must be given an opportunity to resubmit documents or to appeal the decision through the platform's internal review process.

### 4. Verification standards for individual vendors

#### 4.1 Primary identity documents

A member platform must collect at least one of the following primary identity documents from an individual vendor:

(a) an Australian driver licence issued by a state or territory authority;

(b) an Australian passport;

(c) a foreign passport with a valid Australian visa;

(d) an Australian Proof of Age Card issued by a state or territory authority; or

(e) an ImmiCard issued by the Department of Home Affairs.

#### 4.2 Secondary identity documents

Where the primary document does not include a photograph, or where the platform determines that additional evidence is required, the platform must collect at least one secondary document, such as:

**4. Verification standards for individual vendors (cont.)**

**4.2 Secondary identity documents (cont.)**

Examples of acceptable secondary documents include, but are not limited to:

(a) an Australian birth certificate issued by a state or territory Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages;

(b) an Australian citizenship certificate;

(c) a Medicare card;

(d) a bank statement or credit card statement dated within the last three months, showing the vendor's name and residential address;

(e) a utility bill (electricity, gas, water, or telecommunications) dated within the last three months, showing the vendor's name and residential address;

(f) a rates notice from a local council; or

(g) a Centrelink or Department of Veterans' Affairs concession card.

Where a secondary document is used to confirm a residential address, the document must be no more than three months old at the time of submission.

**4.3 Document verification requirements**

(a) A member platform must verify that the document presented is genuine and unaltered, using reasonable technical and procedural measures.

(b) Where a document contains a machine-readable zone (MRZ) or a chip, the platform should read the MRZ or chip if technically feasible.

(c) A platform must check that the name on the primary document matches the name provided by the vendor at registration, allowing for reasonable variations such as middle names, initials, or a change of name evidenced by a marriage certificate or change of name certificate.

(d) Where the vendor's name has changed, the platform must sight the supporting change of name documentation.

(e) A platform must check that the document has not expired. An expired document may not be used for verification, unless the document is a foreign passport accompanied by a valid Australian visa, in which case the passport may be accepted if it was valid at the time the visa was granted.

**4.4 Verification of business vendors**

(a) For a vendor that is a company, a partnership, a trust, or an incorporated association, the member platform must collect:

(i) an Australian Business Number (ABN) or Australian Company Number (ACN), and verify the registration against the Australian Business Register or the Australian Securities and Investments Commission register;

(ii) evidence of the business name, such as a current Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) registration extract, a partnership agreement, or a trust deed;

(iii) the full name, date of birth, and residential address of each individual who owns or controls the business, or who is an authorised signatory on the business account; and

(iv) primary and secondary identity documents for at least one individual who is an authorised signatory, in accordance with clauses 4.1 and 4.2.

(b) Where the vendor is a trust, the platform must also collect the date of the trust deed and the name of the trustee.

(c) Where the vendor is a company, the platform must also collect the names of all directors.

**4.5 Verification of non-individual entities**

Where a vendor is a government body, a registered charity, or a public company listed on a recognised Australian stock exchange, the platform may apply a reduced verification procedure, provided that the platform records the basis for applying the reduced procedure and retains a copy of the supporting evidence.

**4.6 Exemptions**

(a) A member platform may apply to the Committee for an exemption from a specific requirement of this standard. An exemption must be sought in writing and must set out the grounds for the exemption, including any alternative measures the platform proposes to adopt.

documents.title: Investigation into Counterfeit Electronics Spike: Findings and Recommendations
documents.content:
2.1 Scope

The investigation covered the six largest consumer-to-consumer and business-to-consumer online marketplaces operating in Australia: TradeDirect, MarketLoop, BayMart, OzTrade, SellFast, and GreenMarket. The period of interest was 1 October 2022 to 31 March 2023, with comparative baseline data drawn from the preceding six months (April–September 2022).

Product categories in scope were limited to portable consumer electronics with a retail value under $150 AUD, being:
- Portable power banks and chargers
- Wireless earbuds and headphones
- USB wall adaptors and cables
- Smartphone accessories (cases, screen protectors, chargers)

2.2 Methodology

Data was collected from four sources:

1. Platform takedown reports. Each platform provided monthly counts of listings removed for suspected counterfeiting, disaggregated by product category and seller account age at time of listing.
2. Purchaser complaints. MSWG collated complaints lodged with the ACCC and state fair-trading agencies that referenced specific platforms and products.
3. Undercover test purchases. MSWG staff made 142 test purchases of electronics from all six platforms, of which 61 items were subsequently confirmed as counterfeit by independent product authentication testing.
4. Seller onboarding data. Platforms were asked to provide aggregate counts of new seller registrations per month, with a breakdown by declared product category.

Limitations: Data quality varied across platforms. GreenMarket and BayMart provided only quarterly aggregates rather than monthly figures. Seller age data for TradeDirect was incomplete for October 2022, with 14% of new seller records missing a registration date. These gaps are noted in the relevant tables.

---

3. Findings: Overall Counterfeit Listing Trends

Table 1 shows the total number of confirmed counterfeit electronics listings removed by each platform, by quarter.

The MSWG investigation identified TradeDirect as the platform responsible for pattern. Record status: current.

Table 1: Confirmed counterfeit electronics listings removed, by platform and quarter

| Platform     | Q3 2022 (Jul–Sep) | Q4 2022 (Oct–Dec) | Q1 2023 (Jan–Mar) | % change Q3–Q1 |
|--------------|-------------------|--------------------|--------------------|----------------|
| TradeDirect  | 412               | 1,386              | 1,104              | +168%          |
| MarketLoop   | 238               | 402                | 356                | +50%           |
| BayMart      | 156               | 210                | 188                | +21%           |
| OzTrade      | 98                | 142                | 121                | +23%           |
| SellFast     | 74                | 96                 | 88                 | +19%           |
| GreenMarket  | 41                | 55                 | 49                 | +20%           |

Source: Platform takedown reports, MSWG collation.

The Q4 2022 spike on TradeDirect is the dominant feature of the dataset, accounting for 61% of all counterfeit listings removed across the six platforms during that quarter. The Q1 2023 figure for TradeDirect remains elevated above its Q3 baseline.

---

4. Seasonal Pattern Analysis

4.1 Weekly distribution

Weekly takedown data from TradeDirect shows a clear temporal pattern. The first week of November 2022 recorded 142 takedowns, rising to a peak of 318 in the week commencing 12 December 2022. Takedowns remained above 250 per week through the week commencing 2 January 2023, before declining to 96 by the week commencing 30 January 2023. A secondary peak of 148 takedowns occurred in the week commencing 20 February 2023, coinciding with back-to-school advertising.

4.2 Comparison with other platforms

MarketLoop, the platform with the second-highest volume, recorded a peak of 74 takedowns in the week commencing 12 December 2022, less than one-quarter of TradeDirect's peak. MarketLoop's weekly takedown rate was otherwise stable, ranging between 28 and 51 per week across the six-month period.

documents.content:
The onboarding data shows a substantial increase in new seller registrations from October 2022, peaking in December 2022 at 2,740 new registrations — more than double the September figure. The activation of dormant accounts followed a similar trajectory. TradeDirect's own analysis attributes this influx to the pre-Christmas selling season, when many small businesses and individual sellers open accounts to clear stock or offer gift items. The Working Group notes that this seasonal influx of new sellers is the pattern attributed to TradeDirect in the current investigation, though this attribution is provisional and subject to further verification.

The correlation between the onboarding peak and the takedown peak is strong. The week of peak takedowns (commencing 12 December 2022) fell within the month of highest new seller registrations. Of the 318 takedowns in that week, TradeDirect's records indicate that 214 (67%) were listings posted by sellers who had registered within the preceding 30 days. By contrast, in the week commencing 30 January 2023, when takedowns fell to 96, only 31 (32%) were from sellers registered within the preceding 30 days.

4.4 Enforcement lag hypothesis

An alternative explanation considered by the Working Group was that the spike did not reflect a genuine increase in counterfeit listings, but rather a lag in enforcement action. Under this hypothesis, listings that had been present on the platform for some time were only identified and removed in Q4 2022, perhaps due to a backlog or a change in review procedures.

TradeDirect reported that it had not changed its review procedures during the period under examination. The platform's enforcement team confirmed that no additional staff were assigned to counterfeit review in Q4 2022, and that the average time between listing and takedown remained stable at 4.2 days for the period September 2022 to February 2023. The Working Group also reviewed a sample of 150 takedown records from December 2022: in 118 cases, the listing had been posted within 7 days of removal, and in 132 cases within 14 days. Only 6 listings had been active for more than 30 days. This is not consistent with a backlog or enforcement lag explanation.

4.5 Seasonal comparison with prior years

The pattern attributed to TradeDirect is seasonal influx of new sellers. Record status: pending verification.

To assess whether the Q4 2022 spike was unusual or part of a recurring seasonal pattern, the Working Group requested historical takedown data from TradeDirect for the corresponding quarters of 2020 and 2021. TradeDirect's records for these periods are less complete, as the platform only began systematic categorisation of counterfeit electronics listings in March 2021. The available data is set out below.

| Period                     | Takedowns (counterfeit electronics) |
|----------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Q4 2020 (Oct–Dec)          | Not available                       |
| Q1 2021 (Jan–Mar)          | 287                                 |
| Q4 2021 (Oct–Dec)          | 1,050                               |
| Q1 2022 (Jan–Mar)          | 640                                 |
| Q4 2022 (Oct–Dec)          | 1,386                               |
| Q1 2023 (Jan–Mar)          | 1,104                               |

The Q4 2021 figure of 1,050 takedowns suggests that a seasonal increase in counterfeit electronics listings around the Christmas period is not unique to 2022. However, the Q4 2022 figure is 32% higher than the corresponding period in 2021, and the Q1 2023 figure is 73% higher than Q1 2022. The Working Group notes that the 2021 data should be treated with some caution, as TradeDirect's categorisation procedures were still being refined during that period and some listings may have been miscategorised.

4.6 Quality of seller screening

The Working Group also examined whether TradeDirect's seller screening procedures had changed in a way that might have allowed a higher proportion of counterfeit listings to pass through. TradeDirect's onboarding process requires new sellers to provide identification and a bank account in the same name, and to complete a short verification call for listings above a certain value threshold. The platform confirmed that these requirements were unchanged throughout the period under review.

documents.content:
## 4.7 Listing content and image verification

TradeDirect's listing process relies primarily on seller-declared attributes, with image recognition software used to flag listings where the product images appear inconsistent with the declared brand, model, or condition. The Working Group requested details on the volume of listings flagged by this software and the subsequent outcomes, for the period October 2022 to March 2023. TradeDirect advised that the image recognition tool was updated in September 2022 to include a broader set of brand logos and packaging patterns, and that this update may have contributed to a higher detection rate in Q4 2022. The table below summarises the data provided.

| Month       | Listings flagged by image recognition | Takedowns following manual review | Takedowns without flag (seller-reported/other) |
|-------------|---------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Oct 2022    | 412                                   | 289                               | 74                                             |
| Nov 2022    | 538                                   | 371                               | 91                                             |
| Dec 2022    | 601                                   | 428                               | 103                                            |
| Jan 2023    | 447                                   | 302                               | 68                                             |
| Feb 2023    | 389                                   | 261                               | 55                                             |
| Mar 2023    | 351                                   | 244                               | 47                                             |

The Working Group notes that the image recognition tool does not independently confirm a listing as counterfeit; it only generates a flag for human review. The proportion of flagged listings that resulted in takedowns ranged from 68% to 70% across the six months, which is broadly consistent with the platform's historical average of 67%. This suggests that the increase in takedowns in Q4 2022 was not primarily driven by a change in the efficiency of the flagging process, but rather by a higher volume of listings being flagged in the first place.

One limitation of this analysis is that TradeDirect does not retain records of image recognition flags for more than 90 days. As a result, the Working Group was unable to compare flag volumes for the corresponding period in 2021. The platform confirmed that the September 2022 update to the image recognition tool was the only significant change to its listing verification systems during the period under review.

## 4.8 Comparison across product categories

To determine whether the spike in counterfeit electronics was specific to that category or part of a broader trend, the Working Group requested takedown data for three other product categories over the same period: branded footwear, luxury handbags, and automotive parts. These categories were selected because they are commonly targeted by counterfeiters and because TradeDirect's categorisation procedures for these categories have been stable since 2021.

| Category           | Q4 2021 takedowns | Q1 2022 takedowns | Q4 2022 takedowns | Q1 2023 takedowns |
|--------------------|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Branded footwear   | 2,140             | 1,380             | 2,260             | 1,410             |
| Luxury handbags    | 1,890             | 1,120             | 1,970             | 1,180             |
| Automotive parts   | 340               | 210               | 385               | 245               |
| Counterfeit electronics | 1,050         | 640               | 1,386             | 1,104             |

The data indicates that all four categories experienced a seasonal increase in takedowns in Q4 compared with Q1 of the following year, which is consistent with higher consumer demand during the Christmas period. However, the magnitude of the increase varies. For branded footwear, the Q4 2022 figure is 6% higher than Q4 2021; for luxury handbags, the increase is 4%; and for automotive parts, it is 13%. In contrast, counterfeit electronics takedowns increased by 32% over the same comparison. Similarly, the Q1 2023 figures for footwear, handbags, and automotive parts are within 2–5% of their Q1 2022 equivalents, whereas counterfeit electronics takedowns rose by 73%.

# Investigation into Counterfeit Electronics Spike: Findings and Recommendations

**Marketplace Safety Working Group**
**Report to the TradeDirect Trust & Safety Council**

**Report Number:** MSWG-2023-04
**Date:** 18 May 2023
**Status:** Final – for Council adoption at the 24 May 2023 meeting
**Authorising Officer:** M. Chen, Chair, Marketplace Safety Working Group
**Prepared by:** A. Okafor (Policy), R. Patel (Data Analytics), J. Nguyen (Legal)

---

## 5. Analysis of potential contributing factors

The preceding sections established that the spike in counterfeit electronics takedowns in Q4 2022 and Q1 2023 was not explained by changes to listing verification systems, nor by a generalised increase in counterfeiting across other product categories. This section examines four plausible contributing factors in turn: seller behaviour, buyer demand shifts, enforcement intensity, and supply chain disruption. For each factor, the Working Group assessed the available evidence and, where data was insufficient, identified what additional monitoring would be required.

### 5.1 Seller-side factors

A common hypothesis was that a cohort of new sellers had entered the electronics category in late 2022, possibly attracted by the Christmas trading period. The Working Group obtained seller registration data for the electronics category for Q4 2021, Q1 2022, Q4 2022, and Q1 2023. The table below summarises the number of new seller registrations and the proportion of those sellers against whom at least one takedown action was taken within 60 days of registration.

| Period | New seller registrations (electronics) | Sellers with ≥1 takedown within 60 days | Proportion |
|--------|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|------------|
| Q4 2021 | 412 | 38 | 9.2% |
| Q1 2022 | 305 | 21 | 6.9% |
| Q4 2022 | 448 | 41 | 9.2% |
| Q1 2023 | 317 | 24 | 7.6% |

The absolute number of new seller registrations in Q4 2022 was 8.7% higher than in Q4 2021, and the proportion of new sellers attracting takedowns was identical (9.2%) across both Q4 periods. This suggests that while more sellers entered the category, their behaviour, at least as measured by early takedown activity, was not materially different from the prior year. The Working Group therefore considers the seller-entry hypothesis to be weak on its own.

A second seller-side hypothesis concerned repeat offending. If a small number of sellers were responsible for a disproportionate share of the increase, this would point toward enforcement gaps rather than a broad shift. The Working Group examined the concentration of takedowns among the top 20 sellers by takedown count in each period.

| Period | Total electronics takedowns | Share attributable to top 20 sellers |
|--------|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| Q4 2021 | 1,050 | 31% |
| Q1 2022 | 640 | 29% |
| Q4 2022 | 1,386 | 33% |
| Q1 2023 | 1,104 | 36% |

The concentration increased modestly in Q1 2023, with the top 20 sellers accounting for 36% of takedowns compared with 29% in Q1 2022. However, the Working Group notes that this measure can be inflated by legitimate sellers who list many products and are subject to occasional erroneous takedowns. A follow-up review of the Q1 2023 top 20 sellers found that 14 of the 20 had been the subject of at least one successful appeal against a takedown in the previous 12 months, which complicates interpretation. The Group recommends that repeat-offender monitoring be refined to exclude sellers with a high appeal success rate, as detailed in Section 7.

### 5.2 Buyer demand and pricing signals

A second hypothesis was that increased consumer demand for electronics during the Christmas period, combined with supply shortages for certain branded items, had driven buyers toward cheaper alternatives, some of which were counterfeit. The Working Group reviewed internal search and clickstream data for the electronics category for Q4 2021 and Q4 2022. The data was provided by the TradeDirect data science team and covers searches originating from Australian users only.

7.5 Nothing in this clause requires a member platform to verify the business registration of a vendor who is a natural person trading under their own name, provided that the platform has verified the vendor's identity in accordance with clause 4.

8. Verification of Bank Account and Payment Details

8.1 Member platforms must verify that the bank account nominated by a vendor for receiving payments is held in the vendor's name before the vendor's first payout.

8.2 Verification of bank account details must include at least one of the following:

(a) confirmation of the account name against the vendor's verified identity;

(b) a micro-deposit verification, where the platform deposits a small amount into the nominated account and the vendor confirms the amount;

(c) confirmation from the vendor's financial institution, provided that the platform has a written agreement with the institution for this purpose; or

(d) any other method approved by the Policy Review Subcommittee.

8.3 Where a vendor changes their nominated bank account, the member platform must complete verification of the new account before processing any payout to that account. The platform may place a hold of up to five business days on payouts to the new account.

8.4 Member platforms must record the date on which bank account verification was completed and the method used. This record must be retained for at least seven years after the vendor's account is closed.

9. Complaints Handling

9.1 Member platforms must maintain a complaints handling process that is accessible, transparent, and free of charge to vendors and buyers.

9.2 The complaints handling process must allow complaints to be lodged through at least two channels, including an electronic channel, and must provide an acknowledgement of receipt within two business days.

9.3 Member platforms must investigate each complaint promptly and thoroughly, and must provide the complainant with a written outcome of the investigation.

9.4 Under the Complaints Handling Policy 2020, the complaint resolution target is 14 days. Record status: current. This target applies to all complaints received by member platforms, whether the complaint relates to a vendor, a buyer, or the platform's own conduct. The 14-day period runs from the date the complaint is received by the platform.

9.5 Where a complaint cannot be resolved within 14 days, the member platform must notify the complainant in writing, explain the reasons for the delay, and provide an expected resolution date. The member platform must escalate the complaint to a senior staff member who has authority to resolve the matter.

9.6 Member platforms must keep a register of all complaints received, including the date received, the subject matter, the outcome, and the date resolved. The register must be made available to the Policy Review Subcommittee on request.

9.7 Nothing in this clause prevents a member platform from providing a faster resolution time than 14 days, and platforms are encouraged to do so where practicable.

10. Reporting and Audits

10.1 Member platforms must submit a compliance report to the Policy Review Subcommittee on a quarterly basis. The report must include:

(a) the number of vendors verified and re-verified during the quarter;

(b) the number of vendor accounts suspended under clause 5.4 or clause 7.4;

(c) the number of complaints received and the number resolved within 14 days;

(d) the number of complaints not resolved within 14 days, with reasons; and

(e) any other information requested by the Policy Review Subcommittee.

10.2 Reports must be submitted within 20 business days of the end of each quarter. The quarters end on 31 March, 30 June, 30 September, and 31 December.

10.3 The Policy Review Subcommittee may conduct audits of member platforms to assess compliance with this standard. Audits may be announced or unannounced, and may include review of verification records, complaints registers, and other relevant documentation.

10.4 Member platforms must cooperate with any audit and must provide access to records and staff within a reasonable timeframe.

**Status:** Historical document – superseded by Version 3.0 (effective 1 July 2023). Version 2.1 remains the binding standard for all member platforms for the period 14 March 2021 to 30 June 2023, except where a later amendment is expressly noted in the amendment register attached as Schedule C.

---

**17. Transitional Arrangements (continued)**

17.1 Member platforms that were participating in the MarketSafe Program as at the effective date of this standard must achieve full compliance with all new verification requirements within six months of the effective date.

17.2 For the avoidance of doubt, the transitional period in clause 17.1 does not apply to:

(a) the incident notification requirements in clause 11, which apply from the effective date; or

(b) the quarterly reporting requirements in clause 15, which apply from the first full quarter following the effective date.

17.3 Where a member platform considers that it cannot achieve full compliance within the transitional period, it must notify the Policy Review Subcommittee in writing before the end of the transitional period, setting out:

(a) the specific clauses with which it cannot comply;

(b) the reasons for the delay; and

(c) a proposed timeline for achieving compliance, which must not extend beyond 12 months from the effective date.

17.4 The Policy Review Subcommittee may grant an extension under clause 17.3 on such conditions as it considers appropriate, including conditions relating to interim verification measures.

17.5 During the transitional period, member platforms must continue to comply with the Vendor Verification Standard 2019 to the extent that it is not inconsistent with this standard.

**18. Definitions**

In this standard, unless the contrary intention appears:

**Account takeover** means unauthorised access to, or use of, a vendor account by a person other than the registered vendor.

**Biometric verification** means the automated comparison of a physical or behavioural characteristic of an individual against a stored reference, including facial recognition, fingerprint matching, or voice recognition.

**Business day** means a day that is not a Saturday, Sunday, or public holiday in the State or Territory in which the relevant member platform has its principal place of business in Australia.

**Document verification** means the process of checking the authenticity and validity of an identity document using technical and manual checks.

**Identity document** means a document issued by a government authority, or by a body authorised by a government authority, that is commonly accepted as proof of identity in Australia, including:

(a) a driver licence issued under a law of a State or Territory;

(b) an Australian passport;

(c) an ImmiCard issued by the Department of Home Affairs;

(d) a proof of age card issued under a law of a State or Territory; or

(e) any other document approved by the Policy Review Subcommittee for the purposes of this standard.

**Member platform** means an online marketplace that has entered into a participation agreement with the MarketSafe Program and is bound by this standard.

**Sanctions list** means a list of individuals or entities subject to financial sanctions or travel bans administered by the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, or by the United Nations Security Council, as updated from time to time.

**Systemic issue** means a recurring failure in a verification process that affects, or is likely to affect, more than one vendor account or more than one verification transaction.

**Verification transaction** means a single instance of verifying a vendor, including the collection, checking, and storage of verification data.

**Vendor** means a person or entity that offers goods or services for sale on a member platform.

**6. Verification Procedures**

**6.1 General requirements**

A member platform must complete the verification of a vendor before the vendor is permitted to list goods or services for sale. Verification must be completed in accordance with this standard and the member platform's own verification procedure, provided that the member platform's procedure is no less stringent than the requirements set out in this Part.

Each verification transaction must be recorded in a manner that enables the Policy Review Subcommittee (the Subcommittee) to audit the transaction on request. The record must include:

(a) the date and time of the verification transaction (in AEST or AEDT, as applicable);
(b) the type and identifying details of the identity document relied upon;
(c) the outcome of each check performed;
(d) the name and identifier of the person who performed the verification, if performed manually; and
(e) any exception, flag, or referral arising from the verification.

Records must be retained for a period of not less than seven years from the date of the verification transaction.

**6.2 Identity verification of individual vendors**

A member platform must verify the identity of an individual vendor by:

(a) obtaining a clear copy of at least one identity document;
(b) performing a live biometric verification of the vendor against the identity document, unless an exemption applies under clause 6.4;
(c) checking the identity document against the document verification service approved by the Subcommittee for that document type; and
(d) confirming that the name, date of birth, and photograph (where applicable) on the identity document match the information provided by the vendor and the biometric verification.

Where a vendor does not hold an identity document listed in the definition of that term, the member platform may accept two alternative documents that together establish the vendor's identity, provided that:

(a) at least one document includes a photograph of the vendor;
(b) the documents are issued by an Australian government authority or an authority of a recognised foreign government; and
(c) the member platform records the reasons for accepting the alternative documents.

**6.3 Verification of non-individual vendors (business entities)**

Where a vendor is a company, partnership, trust, or other entity, the member platform must verify:

(a) the existence and current status of the entity, by reference to the Australian Business Register, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, or an equivalent register in the jurisdiction of registration;
(b) the identity of each individual who holds a substantial interest in the entity or who is authorised to act on behalf of the entity, in accordance with clause 6.2;
(c) the entity's Australian Business Number (ABN), where the entity has an ABN; and
(d) the entity's registered address and, where different, its principal place of business.

A member platform must not rely solely on a business name registration or an ABN record to verify the identity of the individuals associated with the entity.

**6.4 Biometric verification exemptions**

A member platform may apply to the Subcommittee for an exemption from the biometric verification requirement in clause 6.2(b) where:

(a) the vendor is located outside Australia and cannot reasonably attend a biometric verification session;
(b) the vendor has a recognised disability or condition that prevents the use of the member platform's biometric verification method; or
(c) the vendor is a returning vendor whose identity was previously verified under an earlier version of this standard and whose identity document has not expired.

An exemption is valid for a period of 12 months from the date of grant, unless revoked earlier. The member platform must record the basis for the exemption and review it at each re-verification.

### 1. Purpose and scope

This standard sets out the minimum requirements for verifying the identity of vendors who list goods or services on member platforms. It applies to all member platforms operating in Australia, and to platforms outside Australia where they onboard Australian-based vendors.

The standard is binding on member platforms. The Policy Review Subcommittee (the Subcommittee) is responsible for interpretation, exemptions, and compliance monitoring.

### 2. Definitions

In this standard:

**ABN** means Australian Business Number.

**Biometric verification** means the automated comparison of a live image or video of a vendor against a government-issued identity document containing a photograph.

**Document verification** means the process of checking the authenticity and consistency of identity documents, including against issuing authority records where available.

**Member platform** means any online marketplace that has adopted this standard as a condition of membership of the trust and safety programme.

**Re-verification** means the periodic re-checking of a vendor's identity in accordance with clause 7.

**Subcommittee** means the Policy Review Subcommittee.

**Vendor** means an individual or entity that lists goods or services for sale on a member platform.

### 3. Compliance requirements

#### 3.1 General obligation

Each member platform must implement a vendor verification process that meets or exceeds the requirements of this standard. A platform may adopt stricter requirements where it considers this necessary to manage risk.

#### 3.2 Record keeping

Member platforms must keep the following records for each vendor:

(a) the identity documents collected during verification;

(b) the results of any biometric or document verification checks;

(c) the date and time of each verification event;

(d) the name and identifier of the staff member or system that performed the verification;

(e) any exemption granted under clause 6.4, including the basis for the exemption;

(f) any rejection or escalation, including the reason; and

(g) any communication with the vendor about a failed verification attempt.

Records must be retained for at least seven years after the vendor's account is closed, or longer if required by law.

#### 3.3 Data protection

Member platforms must handle identity documents and verification data in accordance with the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and any other applicable privacy legislation. Identity data must not be used for any purpose other than verification, fraud prevention, and compliance with this standard, unless the vendor has given separate consent.

#### 3.4 Notification of verification decisions

Where a vendor's verification is rejected, the member platform must notify the vendor within five business days and provide a clear statement of the reason for the rejection. The vendor must be given an opportunity to resubmit documents or to appeal the decision through the platform's internal review process.

### 4. Verification standards for individual vendors

#### 4.1 Primary identity documents

A member platform must collect at least one of the following primary identity documents from an individual vendor:

(a) an Australian driver licence issued by a state or territory authority;

(b) an Australian passport;

(c) a foreign passport with a valid Australian visa;

(d) an Australian Proof of Age Card issued by a state or territory authority; or

(e) an ImmiCard issued by the Department of Home Affairs.

#### 4.2 Secondary identity documents

**4. Verification standards for individual vendors (cont.)**

**4.2 Secondary identity documents (cont.)**

Examples of acceptable secondary documents include, but are not limited to:

(a) an Australian birth certificate issued by a state or territory Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages;

(b) an Australian citizenship certificate;

(c) a Medicare card;

(d) a bank statement or credit card statement dated within the last three months, showing the vendor's name and residential address;

(e) a utility bill (electricity, gas, water, or telecommunications) dated within the last three months, showing the vendor's name and residential address;

(f) a rates notice from a local council; or

(g) a Centrelink or Department of Veterans' Affairs concession card.

Where a secondary document is used to confirm a residential address, the document must be no more than three months old at the time of submission.

**4.3 Document verification requirements**

(a) A member platform must verify that the document presented is genuine and unaltered, using reasonable technical and procedural measures.

(b) Where a document contains a machine-readable zone (MRZ) or a chip, the platform should read the MRZ or chip if technically feasible.

(c) A platform must check that the name on the primary document matches the name provided by the vendor at registration, allowing for reasonable variations such as middle names, initials, or a change of name evidenced by a marriage certificate or change of name certificate.

(d) Where the vendor's name has changed, the platform must sight the supporting change of name documentation.

(e) A platform must check that the document has not expired. An expired document may not be used for verification, unless the document is a foreign passport accompanied by a valid Australian visa, in which case the passport may be accepted if it was valid at the time the visa was granted.

**4.4 Verification of business vendors**

(a) For a vendor that is a company, a partnership, a trust, or an incorporated association, the member platform must collect:

(i) an Australian Business Number (ABN) or Australian Company Number (ACN), and verify the registration against the Australian Business Register or the Australian Securities and Investments Commission register;

(ii) evidence of the business name, such as a current Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) registration extract, a partnership agreement, or a trust deed;

(iii) the full name, date of birth, and residential address of each individual who owns or controls the business, or who is an authorised signatory on the business account; and

(iv) primary and secondary identity documents for at least one individual who is an authorised signatory, in accordance with clauses 4.1 and 4.2.

(b) Where the vendor is a trust, the platform must also collect the date of the trust deed and the name of the trustee.

(c) Where the vendor is a company, the platform must also collect the names of all directors.

**4.5 Verification of non-individual entities**

Where a vendor is a government body, a registered charity, or a public company listed on a recognised Australian stock exchange, the platform may apply a reduced verification procedure, provided that the platform records the basis for applying the reduced procedure and retains a copy of the supporting evidence.

**4.6 Exemptions**

(a) A member platform may apply to the Committee for an exemption from a specific requirement of this standard. An exemption must be sought in writing and must set out the grounds for the exemption, including any alternative measures the platform proposes to adopt.
